posts.text:
In 2003, a director made a film about a serial killer nobody could catch. He was sure the killer would watch it. 16 years later, they found him. The truth was darker than the film: he'd been sitting in a prison cell the whole time.

September 1986. Hwaseong, South Korea. A quiet farming region where nothing ever happens. A 71 y/o woman visits her daughter, sets off for home, and never arrives. Days later, she's found dead.

It was the beginning of the darkest chapter in Korean crime history.

Over the next five years, 10 women were murdered. Different ages, different villages, same signature. Women stopped walking home alone. Fear settled over the rice fields like fog.

It became the biggest manhunt in the country's history. Over 21,000 suspects investigated. 40,000+ people fingerprinted. And still, almost nothing. One woman survived an attack and could only describe him as skinny, with a low voice. That was all they had.

A rumour spread that the killer only struck women in red on rainy nights. So female officers put on red and walked the dark roads alone, as bait.

He never came.

The pressure was unbearable, and it showed. Suspects were dragged in and interrogated, some allegedly beaten. In 1989, police announced they had solved the 8th murder. They arrested Yoon Sung-yeo, a 22-year-old repairman. He confessed and was sentenced to life.

Keep his name in mind.

The killings stopped in 1991. No arrest. No answers.

Then in 2003, a young Bong Joon-ho, making only his second feature and years away from Parasite, turned the case into Memories of Murder.

It's no slick thriller. Song Kang-ho plays a small-town cop who solves cases by gut instinct, intimidation and, when that fails, his fists. His team beats confessions out of suspects and arrests whoever looks guilty enough. You laugh at their incompetence, until you realise you're watching a system so terrified it will break anyone to make the fear stop.

The film ends with no killer. Because in 2003, there wasn't one.

Then comes the final shot. Years later, the detective is a family man selling juicers. He drives past the field where it all began and stops. A little girl tells him a man was just there, looking at the same spot. What did he look like? "Just... ordinary." Song Kang-ho turns and stares straight into the camera.

Straight at you.

Bong later explained why. He believed the killer would sit in a theatre and watch the film about his own crimes. He wanted the detective to look out at the audience, at the killer, and the killer to look back.

September 2019. Evidence that had sat in storage for nearly three decades was sent for modern DNA testing. The result came back with a match.

His name was Lee Choon-jae.

He wasn't hiding. He had been in prison since 1994, serving life for murdering his sister-in-law. When the film hit theatres, the man that final shot was staring at was already behind bars.

When his face was finally released, people noticed something eerie: he looked strikingly like the film's prime suspect.

He confessed to all 10 Hwaseong murders, and 4 more nobody had ever linked to him. Fourteen lives.

But the statute of limitations had expired. He could not be charged for a single one.

Later, he was asked about that final stare. He said he had never thought about how it made him feel.

And Yoon Sung-yeo?

Lee confessed to the 8th murder too, the one Yoon went to prison for. Yoon had been innocent all along. His confession had been forced out of him through abuse, exactly like the scenes Bong put on screen.

He spent nearly 20 years in prison for another man's crime. He was released on parole in 2009, still carrying the label of murderer. In 2020, Korean police publicly apologised. That December, a court finally cleared his name.

He went in at 22. He was declared innocent at 53.

A film that stared into a killer's eyes.
A killer locked away the entire time.
An innocent man who lost 20 years to the very system the film portrayed. 

🎬 Memories of Murder

🚨🇺🇲 Jensen Huang is OUT at Nvidia, but Silicon Valley is practically BEGGING for him to come back.

Employees are openly mourning his departure. One engineer even declared that Nvidia had lost its SOUL.

Elon signed a petition demanding his reinstatement. Major investors are urging the board not to rush into replacing him.

And there's a reason for all this loyalty.

One startup founder says he cold-emailed Huang with an AI idea and got a reply in SEVEN MINUTES. Huang then approved a team to work on it at Nvidia HQ.

The man built Nvidia into the backbone of the AI industry. Now he's gone amid allegations involving extramarital affairs and a suspected Chinese intelligence connection that hasn't even been proven.

No evidence has been established that Huang knowingly compromised Nvidia.

Silicon Valley seems willing to forgive his personal mistakes. 

Will the man come back after all?

BREAKING: Samsung reportedly plans to make chips for SpaceX’s Starlink satellites in Austin, Texas. 

Samsung is investing $1.9 billion to expand its Austin chip factory, with the planned operations targeted to begin by 2030, according to Seoul Economic Daily.

The chip, called STM32V8, is already used in Starlink’s mini laser system. SpaceX’s Starlink engineering team has praised the chip’s performance.

The chips are currently manufactured in France. The reported Texas plan would add American production capacity for a key component behind Starlink’s satellite communications.

The national debt is growing at an unprecedented pace, and almost no one in Washington is prepared to stop it, per the WSJ.

Debt held by the public is now larger than the entire US economy for the first time since World War II, and interest payments alone top $1 trillion a year. The Congressional Budget Office projects debt will reach 120% of GDP by 2036, well above the postwar record.

BREAKING: Former White House and Pentagon official Douglas MacKinnon calls for an end to political attacks on Elon Musk, saying “our very survival may depend on him.”

• Humanity’s future is vulnerable as long as we live on only one planet. War, an asteroid strike or another major disaster could threaten civilization.

• Elon’s mission is to help humans live on other planets, giving future generations a better chance of surviving if disaster strikes Earth.

• His work toward a permanent human presence in space could become one of his most important contributions to humanity.

• People can disagree with his politics and still recognize the value of what he is trying to achieve.

• MacKinnon argues that Elon deserves the time and freedom to focus on this mission.

Elon is working toward a future where humanity can live beyond Earth and explore the stars. His determination to make that possible deserves recognition and support.

Tens of thousands of homeowners face a payment shock as their adjustable-rate mortgages reset, per the WSJ.

About 186,000 ARMs are set to reset next year, according to data from ICE. The typical borrower’s payment will rise about $645 a month at the first reset.

The hardest hit are people who took out seven-year ARMs in 2020, when rates were near record lows. Their median monthly payment is set to jump 43%, or $1,269, with some going from rates below 3% to closer to 8%.

ARMs make up only about 5% of active mortgages, and today’s versions have more safeguards than those that fueled the 2008 crash.
